requirements.requirement: Run a healthy three-member etcd cluster across node1, node2, node3 holding application keys
requirements.summary: etcd 3.5.17 was bootstrapped across all three nodes; member list shows all three members started, endpoint health reports all three healthy, and four /app/* keys were written and confirmed readable directly from node3's own endpoint.

requirements.requirement: node3's member is permanently lost / unrecoverable (precondition for the replacement scenario)
requirements.summary: etcd was stopped, disabled, and its data directory wiped on node3; subsequent health checks show node1 and node2 remain healthy (quorum preserved) while node3's endpoint is unreachable/connection refused, directly demonstrating the simulated permanent loss.

requirements.requirement: Replace the lost member with a working member on the same system (node3), restoring three healthy members
requirements.summary: The dead member (d4fa53f781f3013) was removed via etcdctl, a new member (baac6b44d3dadfc6) was added for node3, and etcd was restarted there with initial-cluster-state=existing. Post-join member list, endpoint health, and endpoint status all show 3/3 healthy members with matching raft term/applied-index across nodes.

requirements.requirement: Existing application keys remain intact after the replacement
requirements.summary: All four /app/* keys were read directly from the replaced node3 endpoint and match the original values written before the simulated loss.

overall_summary: The executor built the three-member etcd cluster (none pre-existed), loaded application keys, then directly demonstrated the full lost-member replacement scenario: node3 stopped/wiped with quorum preserved on node1/node2, dead member removed, a new member added and started on node3 as a full (non-learner) member, and cluster health plus all application keys confirmed intact from node3's own endpoint afterward. Evidence for every material outcome is direct and specific (member lists, endpoint health, raft indices, key reads) rather than inferred from configuration alone. The independently-required provider-wide node-restart protocol was also completed on all three nodes with genuine boot-id transitions and post-reboot recovery of etcd health and data, though this is supplemental evidence outside the public task contract.
limitations: Package-health checks were unavailable (timed out) at every snapshot phase on all three nodes, so native package-manager consistency cannot be independently verified.

The node-restart protocol, while well-evidenced with real boot-id transitions and recovered state on all three nodes, is not itself part of the public task contract and is treated as supplemental evidence only.
Minor /tmp residue (etcd tarball and extracted install directory) from the install step was not cleaned up on any node, though this is low-risk and non-destructive.

operational_hygiene.summary: All state-changing commands traced back to a clear purpose: chronyc clock corrections were a necessary prerequisite (TLS downloads were failing due to ~9-day clock drift, directly diagnosed via cmd-b67c9eaa290d4af1 and cmd-1ba5d2e997fe4739/cmd-bf09c2d7cf904f03 showing expired-cert failures); etcd install, user/dir creation, systemd units, and firewalld port openings on 2379/2380 were all required for the cluster; the node1 'systemctl enable --now etcd' timeout (cmd-932e0060441745ba, rc=1) was a transient startup timing issue immediately corrected by a restart (cmd-2df4c9ff722c41ec) with no lasting failure (after_executor snapshot shows zero failed services on all nodes). The member-remove/member-add/data-wipe sequence on node3 was the core task action, not incidental. The only residue is the downloaded etcd tarball and extracted install directory left in /tmp on all three nodes (visible in after_executor temporary-files diff) — a bounded, low-risk, non-destructive leftover from a legitimate install step, not fully cleaned up afterward.
